The "Headcount Tax": Penalizing you as your team grows. The Data Sovereignty Risk: Handing read-only API tokens, employee directories, and internal system logs over to third-party US cloud sub-processors. So, as a software engineer, I built an alternative: Kanuga Shield. Instead of routing everything through a heavy, expensive external SaaS cloud, we built a sovereign, local-first continuous compliance engine. How it Works Under the Hood: 100% Local Architecture: Runs locally via a Node.js Express backend and encrypted SQLite databases (auth.db, evidence_vault.db) on your machine or private enclave. Zero external cloud dependencies. Encrypted Credential Vault: All API keys (AWS, GCP, GitHub, Okta, Rippling) are secured at rest using AES-256-GCM. Continuous Controls Evaluation: Automated telemetry mapping live infrastructure and identity checks against SOC 2 (Trust Services Criteria), ISO 27001:2022 (Annex A), and HIPAA. Tamper-Evident Evidence Vault: Every scan computes a cryptographic SHA-256 hash of the raw proof payload so external auditors can verify evidence integrity instantly. Dedicated Auditor Room: Time-bounded, read-only access tokens (7, 30, or 90 days) for third-party CPA firms (Schellman, Coalfire, etc.) to review evidence without exposing your admin dashboard. Pricing: No sales calls, no hidden tiers, and no headcount taxes. Just a flat $5,000/year all-in with all frameworks unlocked on day one. I’d love to hear from other technical founders or security engineers here: How are you handling compliance automation without burning your seed runway on legacy tools? - I am sceptical about superpower theory in application to todays situation. Not many people are aware that the the Non-Aligned Movement is the second largest international organisation after the United Nations. It was founded during the cold war, by newly independent colonies, when the Western Superpowers and the Eastern superpowers tried to drag them into their conflicts and demanded that every country choose a side. Concerned about losing their independence again, they joined hands to tell the superpowers that while they respected their powers NAM wouldn't co-operate with them in thier conflict, nor take sides unless it was to protect their own self-interests or sovereignty. It helped many countries survive the cold war without getting entrapped in it. You are partly right that its relevance waned a bit in the 20th century. That happened because after the collapse of the USSR, the world became Unipolar ( https://foreignpolicy.com/2025/05/26/how-america-blew-its-un... ), with the US dominating the world. This however was temporary as the economic rise of China and Russia, and emerging powers like Germany, India, Brazil etc. made international politics a multi-polar one again. But what really brought the reality of superpower politics (and NAM) to the fore again, was the Ukraine conflict. NAM members recognized it immediately as a proxy war between NATO West and Russia (+China) when they were again pressured to take side "in the name of the Ukrainians". It immediately reeked of cold war politics to most of us in the developing world ( Why some countries don’t want to pick a side in Russia’s war in Ukraine - https://www.vox.com/23156512/russia-ukraine-war-global-south... ). So no, superpower political theory is indeed a reality even today, just as it was responsbile for both the World Wars. And in some way, the Ukraine conflict is a continuing remnant of this. As I see it, the reason why Europe has had so many military conflicts between its superpowers and emerging powers is because the lack of natural barriers make it easy for a land army to invade each other. (For example, the Himalayas provide some natural protection from a Chinese invading army to India and its Himalyan neighbours). World War 1 and 2, and the improvement in military technologya nd modern warfare made this even easier. And post WW2, as the Western superpowers allied against Russia, both faced the same dilemma - how can we slow down an invading army from the otherside to better defend ourselves. The solution both realised was to use the Eastern European countries as "buffer" between them. Whoever was able to win them over to their side, or control them, could use them as temporary shield against the others army. This is why NATO and Russia fight over the Eastern European countries, and try to control them. Where countries had experienced leaders, who were able to unite their people behind them, Russia and NATO smartly avoided conflict over them when such countries joined either side. But where a country was nascent (like most ex-Soviets), the political leaders weak, and the people thus not united behind them, the superpowers blatantly abused their powers to control them, even if it means dividing them between themselves. That is what we see happening in Ukraine - Western superpowers have West Ukraine, and Russia controls East Ukraine. (The worst case is ofcourse another World War). (And I am not talking about this out of my ass - the West has political and military papers on this subject, written a decade or two ago, and they too conclude that the obvious outcome of a war over Ukraine would be that Russia will grab and retain the Eastern parts and Crimea, while Ukraine would shrink to its Western parts)

I don't think the concept of natural language reasoning tokens is here to stay Current open source LLMs have an emergent structure where the first couple layers transform the input into some internal representation. Then the middle does multiple reasoning steps, and the end transforms it back to one output token. You can repeat the middle to get a stronger, slower model, so it is abstract reasoning. And Anthropic had a blog post about actually looking at what the middle does and mapping it back to concept for inspection With that in mind, what's the point of reasoning tokens? They throw rich internal state away, for the benefit of inspectability and variable-length reasoning. But now that we understand the internal structure better we can dynamically vary how many loops the model spins through those middle layers, and still get enough insight into what's happening by decoding internal state. This takes some reengineering of model architecture and inference engines (especially to still get good batch performance), but the potential benefits seem to big to ignore

I want to preface what I'm about to say with the fact that I believe super intelligence is (by some reasonable definition) more likely than not to arrive some time next year. However, today's models have extremely jagged intelligence even within fields it's extremely capable in. Like most people here, I use Claude and other models daily and I used them primarily in the context of building a very complex software project. Claude is brilliant at writing code at, in very clean and well defined codebases, where its being asked to build something that fits well within the preexisting patterns. Someone non-technical who does a lot of vibe coding recently asked why I couldn't just tell Claude to go build some feature into the project and call it a day? And it's genuinely hard to explain to people who are not both experts broadly in the field and experts in the specifics of the problem why this such a bad idea. And annoyingly it's not that Claude won't produce something that works, it will produce something that makes several extremely bad assumptions and defensively codes in those assumptions. And even when you explain this, the question then changes to, "yeah, but you could just ask Claude to fix that". My default way of working today is to start 90% of my projects by simply asking in a few paragraphs what I want, seeing what Claude builds then spending half a day working through it, explaining all the wrong assumptions it's made, then reaching a clean and maintainable solution at the end. However, I have been on the other side of this and I've felt magic of Claude when I've got it to write code I don't really understand. On the surface it seems to be able to do everything I ask stupidly fast. It's better than any human you could ever work with. But who knows what it's doing under the hood... My guess is that you simply can't keep building like that for long because while it will do everything you ask, the foundations of what it's building on are basically non-existent – and anyone whose worked on a serious software project before knows the foundations of any software are by far the most important things in the long-term robustness and maintainability of the project. I guess what I'm saying is that many people who are non-experts in the field or non-exports in the specific problem within the fields they're asking AI to do things are largely delusional about what AI can and can't do. It absolutely can create a simple CRUD app, but it will not build a complicated distributed system and process millions of requests a day with five 9s of uptime. Pretty unlikely they'd be into adding a new ZWJ pattern for bordering characters since it's awful given unicode's main goal is interoperability. If you copy text out of your terminal, those characters come with it and probably won't render correctly in non-terminal applications (which don't have monospaced text cells), so you'll just see the ? missing character symbol between every letter. (Possibly overstruck onto the previous character depending on handling for the ZWJ.) I guess the other way to look at this would be "should the background colour be a unicode ZWJ pattern?"... probably not. The border (and colour) is a property of the terminal cell rather than the actual characters IMO. It's not like `X + ZWJ + LEFT-BORDER` has any unique encoded meaning. This is the right idea, but it's actually not that simple unfortunately: Trusted Publishing relies on per-IdP claims that are more precise than the `sub` claim (because doing pattern matching on the `sub` claim is brittle and prone to security problems). So we require publisher providers (OIDC IdPs) to provide distinct claims that we can match on. For GitHub and GitLab that's things like the repository name, workflow filename, etc., while for others it might be distinct username and immutable ID claims, etc. This is all downstream of OIDC-driven federation being a much weaker and more bespoke process than all parties would like it to be. I think the discourse around this could be much improved by people taking the time to understand these complexities and why they pose a challenge to groups with limited engineering resources (like PyPI).

How it works: It reads 55 news feeds from 51 outlets on six continents, including state media from parties to the conflicts. Claude pulls out specific claims about the world’s biggest stories and labels each one by how well-supported it is: single source, one side only, corroborated or conflicting. A second, separate Claude pass checks every draft. Plain code then rejects any claim whose cited source isn’t actually in that day’s feeds. The theme of this piece is, in fact, "don't absolutize your own standards" — that successful people forget the contingency of their success, forget the situation and context of their judgment, and treat it as a universally correct judgment. But the problem lies in the writing itself that carries this piece's theme. A doctor can smoke while telling a patient that smoking is bad — that's not a problem at all. Honestly, everyone has that degree of contradiction in a homepage essay. So do I. But separate from that, the difficulty in reading this piece is that if you're going to demand intellectual humility, you should at least be consistent within the text. You can criticize the act of reinforcing one's own standards outside one's field. The problem is that it's hard when, within the text, the author violates the very standards he set. Joe Schmoe vs. the Engineer: Why AI Democratized Construction, Not Trust. I can't read or write a line of Python, PyTorch, .NET 10, HTML, or C++ by hand. My background isn't computer science, it's twenty-plus operational jobs across kitchens, warehouses, construction, and CAD drafting. Yet over the past few months, treating AI as a constrained compiler instead of a chatbot, I mapped, built, and automated a multi-language software infrastructure solo. On paper, I look like the edge case people cite when claiming engineers are obsolete. If someone with zero coding literacy can orchestrate runtimes, neural pipelines, backends, and web apps almost autonomously, why does the industry still need engineers? Living through that build proved the opposite. AI automated typing syntax, not systems engineering. Construction got cheap, while human validation and trust became the scarcest resources in tech. The Blindness Tax When an experienced engineer uses AI, they can read the diff. They know where memory leaks hide, how threads collide, and when an OS buffer saturates under load. As Joe Schmoe, every file across C++, .NET, or Python is a black box. I can't look at code and tell if it's clean or silently corrupting state. So I paid the blindness tax; enforcing hard architectural boundaries upfront and building external telemetry probes to test binaries against the OS kernel and hardware. Generating code fast isn't shipping verified software fast. When anyone can spin up prototypes in a weekend, feeds flood with unverified noise, and human attention becomes the bottleneck. The Scientific Method and the Engineer's Moat In science, a hypothesis isn't proven just because it ran on a garage workbench. Proof takes skeptical peers, people who normally argue and tear ideas apart, testing boundaries independently and reaching consensus. Software works the same way. AI can emit thousands of lines of code, and an outsider can wire up a stack, but AI can't grant itself credibility. It can't face an auditor, take legal accountability in production, or vouch for a system in peer review. That's the engineer's real moat: familiarity, workflow mastery, and established trust networks. Engineers speak their peers' dialect, know production failure modes, and hold the keys to validation rooms outsiders knock on. Pair that intuition with a disciplined AI workflow, and they skip the blindness tax. The Open Question In a moment of radical honesty, my only commercial gain from publishing this is getting direct feedback on two puzzles: First, for someone who can't read or write code, how do you recommend proving on your own that the code is sound before asking an outsider to review it? Second, if you're evaluating an unknown, closed-source vendor with zero pedigree; whose proprietary code can't be inspected, leaving only empirical evidence—what specific proof earns your trust?

For anyone actually considering this $200k+ setup for home or even small business use the power usage and noise is extreme. 1.6kw each with the fans to match. 600tokens/s at concurrency 16 is not what you need for home use or even sub 100 employee business use either. Really reconsider please (do you seriously need people to tell you this?). I get tech wages are high and you can probably afford this but seriously. Right now there’s no great solution to the frontier or near frontier models for home use. But there are cards and options coming in 2027. For now just accept that you run qwen 37b or similar. What’s coming in 2027 that changes this and why i implore you to wait? Well for these models you need massive amounts of memory and memory bandwidth. The solution above gets this by using expensive HBM spread over enough cards with enough compute to give a ridiculous tok/s. For home use you’d actually be happier with a single GPU that had lots of cheap memory to hold the weights and just enough memory bandwidth to feed that single gpu and no more. This in theory gets you close to 50tok/s on GLM 5.3 if it existed. In 2027 there’s expected to be multiple HBF (high bandwidth flash) options incoming. High bandwidth flash has ~10x the latency of HBM but that actually doesn’t matter much for inference. Inference is latency tolerant and local inference time to first token beats over the internet time to first token no matter what you do in any case. The bandwidth and amount of memory is the blocker. In 2027 there’s expected to be many multi terabyte HBF options coming. NAND/NOR flash is massively cheaper than RAM per byte (multiple states per logical unit so it’s denser) and it’s not that hard to wire it in a more parallel way to increase its bandwidth. Nvidia has the Kioxia solutions and Sandisk, Samsung, Tenstorrent, Mythic have also previewed HBF with GPUs to do local inference on the open source frontier models at reasonably high tok/s. Even if HBF is sold for 10x the price per terabyte of todays flash that’s still an extremely small fraction of the price of any other option right now. Make do with the subscriptions for now. Don’t go crazy trying to run the frontier at home today. We should have something much better solutions are coming.

Phased copy is the right instinct, but in practice the data is usually lost before any recovery tool runs, not during it. Two rules matter more than the tool choice: never write to the source device, and never let the OS "repair" it on mount. A dirty NTFS volume gets automatic $LogFile replay or chkdsk on Windows, and chkdsk will delete directory entries it decides are orphaned, which is often the difference between a recoverable tree and a pile of carved files. On macOS, attach with hdiutil -readonly -nomount and read blocks; do not let Finder touch it. The second rule: image first, recover from the image. A failing drive gives you a shrinking budget of reads, and every directory walk over the $MFT spends it. A ddrescue-style two pass - large blocks over the healthy run, then 512b only over the holes - usually salvages more than one linear pass, because re-reading a bad sector 30 times is how a head finishes off a platter. If you want a feature request: a resume map file for the phased copy so an interrupted run does not restart from byte zero, and a per-pass block size. Both are cheap, and they are what people actually need on a 2TB drive that is dying.

The first example I gave where you piece together garbled reception is an example of an advisory, non-required communication at a non-towered airfield. The communication isn’t required and just serves as a backup to standard VFR flying. At some fields you aren’t even required to have a radio in the aircraft. Reading between the garbled lines isn’t an issue for these purposes. There’s redundancy built in for critical comms. For critical messages (e.g. “cleared to land”, ) the receiving party reads back what they heard. If a controller doesn’t get the right readback with all of the details, they will correct it. You do occasionally get errors that aren’t caught, or someone that does a readback and then has a brain fart and does something that they aren’t supposed to, but that’s inherent to humans in the system. Also, keep in mind that what you hear on liveATC is not what the pilots and ATC hear. Typically, you get much better reception because you are either on the ground transmitting to an antenna on a tower right next to you, or you are transmitting from thousands of feet up. It’s not unusual at all to hear crystal clear radio calls from 100 miles away. The comms system is surprisingly robust, especially since it can degrade gracefully. AM is much easier to receive at low signal strengths, if there’s some sort of emergency in the tower, they can and have just sent a guy out with binoculars and a handheld to get people on the ground. If you have an electrical issue in the plane, you can grab a backup handheld out of a bag, etc. AM radios have been standard since WWII so all planes have the same equipment. Pilots and aviation regulators think a lot about safety, but replacing the aviation radio system is just not something that comes up.

The software methodology of the future will look a lot like Milt Bryce's PRIDE. Milt realized as early as the 1970s, if not long before, that programmers had way too much power in an organization because most organizations adopted a "tool-oriented approach" to computer technology: here's a tool, how do we make use of it? They let the programmers run wild, and the result was software that was a buggy mess. What's needed is a management-oriented approach in which the management of the company calls the shots on what's needed for the company to function. In PRIDE, the systems analyst is centered. This is explicitly a business role, not a technical role, and their job is to understand the business in such a way that the information systems (not programs, nor apps) that drive the business can be described in diagrams and text. Only once the requirements, definitions of terms, and data definitions have been established and standardized can the implementation phase begin. Bryce estimated that if you're not spending 65% of the effort in systems analysis and only 15% of the effort in programming, you're doing it wrong. This is how grown-ups did information systems for decades . And then the internet happened, "hacker culture" happened, and the programmers were back in the driver's seat, producing things like "Agile". Now we have AI, and to quote another commenter elsewhere in the thread, the programmers have had their tails cut off. That 15% number asymptotically approaches zero. Become a business person, not a software engineer. They are the ones who will drive things forward in the agentic era.

The Anthropic and OAI APIs report token usage (input, output, and in some cases reasoning/thinking). The input tokens consist of the system prompt, the user input/messages, and any other context data. Given the same model the only variable is the token count. The more tokens, the more passes through the LLM (to generate the next output token), the more energy used. It's well known that non-English text consumes more tokens [1], [2] and thus more energy. This is due to two factors: 1. Latin script languages having different character pairings to English and modified characters, including language features like modifying verbs for person/tense/etc. (e.g. Spanish); 2. Non-Latin scripts that take more bytes to represent in UTF-8 and (esp. for ideographic and syllabic languages like Chinese, Japanese, and Korean) have lower common character pair sequences, meaning shorter tokens for those scripts and thus more tokens for a given text sequence. Reading this thread makes me realize that seemingly no one has heard the basic, mundane case for why NVIDIA would want to do so much "circular financing" as a matter of totally normal business strategy. This may not be the whole story, but it's worth understanding. Because of bottlenecks in the supply chain, NVIDIA knows it is going to sell 100% of its inventory. They could raise prices quite a bit more, but then their only customers would be hyperscalers (building competing chips) and possibly OpenAI and Anthropic. NVIDIA is willing to forgo present day profits for the strategic value of keeping its customer base diverse and promoting the network effects of e.g. CUDA. Instead of quoting a lower price per GPU to neoclouds and startups, they finance purchases of chips, but the two are roughly equivalent (financing means NVIDIA takes on more risk, but has more upside and locks in future demand). It is in their commercial interest to have many competing buyers of their chips. Obviously this creates fun mechanisms for fraud and wacky accounting (and I'm agnostic as to whether that's happening here), but it's worth knowing about the boring/obvious story before donning your tinfoil hat.

My very first professional gig in the mid-80s was on a classified ad-taking application for what were then called penny-savers, physical newspaper-like publications that were nearly 100% classifieds. Penny-savers would be distributed in boxes around urban centres and could be very profitable. Our app ran on MP/M, a multi-user CP/M variant. And when it was time to go to print, our code generated PS directly, there was no "printer driver" or abstraction of any kind. We sold our customers two Apple LaserWriters each, because if one went down just before going to print they'd be screwed. We would print on both in parallel for speed, but could fall back to just one. And the printed ads? Somebody over in the print shop would cut them out in strips and then paste those strips up to be photographed for the printing press. We didn't have full end-to-end digital yet. PS wasn't easy, but it was very grokkable.

Neither operators nor overloading are abstractions, and they offer no operation at a higher level. An abstraction is something that creates an equivalence class among multiple implementations, and that's not the case here. First, operators are clearly not an abstraction because they offer a 1-1 correspondence: Instead of `x + y` you write `plus(x, y)`. It's just a different notation. Overloading also isn't an abstraction because, as you pointed out, the resolution is statically known, and again, there's a 1-1 relationship. Indeed, it's just name mangling. Instead of writing `plus_int_int(x, y)` you write `plus(x,y)` and the compiler adds the `int_int` for you. There's no doubt operators and/or overloading have some convenience advantages, but there's also no doubt they have some disadvantages, which is why some languages disallow one or both, regardless of how high or low-level they are. But Zig also has some special reasons to prevent overloading, because the language is built around compile-time introspection. So you can have just a single `plus` for multiple types, but the static dispatch is explicitly controlled by the implementation of `plus`. This means that all resolution is always local or uses unique names. I'm not saying you have to personally like it. Zig and Rust both aim at different preferences so that people may prefer one over the other. But there is no difference in expressivity (but there very much is between assembly or even C and either one of Zig or Rust). Rust, like C++, chooses to favour implicitness over explicitness, and Zig chooses the opposite. Both have pros and cons, and neither is universally superior to the other.

My experiences with LLM's and coding harnesses has improved over the past year or so, but its shortcomings has stayed the same. It produces code that's technically correct, but there's always these subtle issues that would blow up into large issues as time goes on. If an LLM generates 100 lines of code for me, I usually end up rewriting around 90 of them. I could spend my time writing skills files to tell the LLM what it should or should not do, but you run the risk of increasing the context window to the point where the LLM forgets it. At a certain point you have to ask yourself, if I know what needs to be done and how to do it, why am I spending time arguing with the LLM instead of just writing the code myself? The part that I find extremely valuable is using LLM's as a replacement for searching code documentation. If you're new to something, you don't always know how to phrase your search query. The LLM's do an excellent job at translating your novice-level language into the precise terms you need. This saves a lot of people's times. You don't have to ask your question on a forum or to your colleague, saving not just your time, but everyone else's time. That's a big gamechanger. We can spend more time on the task you care about and not on all these tertiary side-trips. What I find extraordinarily disappointing, however, is the industry's reaction was not "Oh wow, look at how much more productive we can make our programmers.". The industry's first reaction was to tokenmaxx and make the LLM's do everything, from writing code, submitting issues, design, etc. It leads to codebases that seem fine on the surface, but as you study the code, you find all sorts of issues. As these issues get discovered, the LLM then has to fix a bunch of different code, which leads to these infamous thousand-line PR/MR's. Even if we LLM's produce code that works, remember that the quality of the LLM's output degrades when the context window reaches a certain point size, which will start costing you more in terms of technical debt, bugs, and the literal token cost. It's also worth pointing out that companies that provide LLM's are still not profitable, so when the arms race between Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic settles, we're going to see the real cost to run these LLM code harnesses, and it just might make you pause think before reaching for the LLM again. On the other hand, if the hardware situation gets fixed, running your models locally would be a viable option, so you only have to worry about the upfront costs and the electricity bill. With all that said, I think there's a bright future with LLM's. They are extremely good at pattern matching, and I think the real business value is in the use-cases that fits cleanly into that role. LLM's might not be the best at writing code, but they're exceptional at finding issues with your code. Case in point, OpenAI recently published a ton of fixes for root privilege exploits in the Linux kernel. I think spending our time constructing and training LLM's on how to discover issues for your particular domain will provide far more value that simply having the LLM write code for you.

And while we're at it, a better TERM variable, not the "user-agent header" of terminals that it is now. To be more precise, TERM contains a single name, a key to index terminfo, a database of all known terminals and their capabilities. It assumes that such database is up to date and that every app has access to it, which is not always true, especially on non-unix platforms. However, apps have begun using the name "as is", comparing it against known strings, e.g. "xterm", which led many terminals to advertise themselves as xterm just to ensure compatibility with existing apps. A truly meaningful substitute for TERM would be a "semantic TERM", a variable that, setting apart the name of the terminal, focuses on the capabilities it offers. Not the complete set of properties listed in terminfo (we can give most of them for granted, today), but just the subset that differentiates modern terminals, like colors, kitty's protocol, OSC133, and a few others.

> The goal of raspberry pi's was to have a standard GPIO connected to a moderately powerful and cheap computer for educational purposes. At first it was a blessing that the Raspberry Pi gained popularity as a general purpose computer, not just for education and embedded applications. The additional demand and popularity brought more money and development attention to the ecosystem. At some point, which I could never really put my finger on, this general purpose computer popularity grew so large that the embedded systems and educational aspects of Raspberry Pi seemed almost forgotten by the mainstream users. At a local in-person meetup group it was a running theme for people to brag about how many Raspberry Pis they owned for different purposes and to boast about using them for applications where they didn’t really fit. In person I’ve heard more about Raspberry Pi NAS systems (where people are always disappointed with the performance and the price of forcing a Pi into this role) or Raspberry Pi Kubernetes clusters (which mostly sat idle and could have been replaced by a single PC with more RAM). This reached such a critical mass that it almost seemed like the mainstream discussion forgot the original purpose of the Pi and thought it was literally just another computer, but small. Most people who tried to use it for this purpose were left slightly frustrated by how it didn’t perform like they wanted a computer to perform. So now every discussion about Raspberry Pi attracts comments about how nobody should buy a Pi when you can buy a NUC or laptop or some other used piece of hardware and it’s so much “better”. This is the right advice for a lot of people who wanted a powerful general computer but bought a Pi instead, but it’s also furthering the misunderstanding of what the Pi is for. The real advice is that everyone should be shopping for the right tool for the job. There are a lot of cool applications for the Pi where a NUC or old laptop or phone doesn’t make sense because you actually need the compact size, the low-level I/O, or some other feature. However anyone who can put a NUC or laptop side by side with a Raspberry Pi and consider them both viable options for their project probably shouldn’t have been looking at a Raspberry Pi to begin with.

A fun article but it is incomplete. It misses out on the company's height. In the early days it has its own server OS, 3Com 3+Share. It was a multitasking file server OS and it was based on MS-DOS. Yes really. An internally multitasking server stack on DOS. I became expert in it in my first job and my 3rd job leant heavily on that and my skills. It used the MS LAN Manager stack over NetBEUI. It inherited DOS limitations like 32MB partitions. On PC servers everything had to for into 640kB of RAM and natively it could not use XMS, only EMS. 3Com offered a range of dedicated network file server boxes, the 3Server. The first was an 80186 and later the 3Server3 with a 386. Then it got big into OS/2 and released 3Com 3+Open. The multitasking stuff obviated by OS/2 1.0's own built in multitasking but now it was multiprotocol and the server could run other stuff too. The 3Server had no display, no port for one, no keyboard connector. It could only be administered over the network. It did have a little 1-line LCD display for showing a status message, accessible via a DOS device driver for showing custom messages. A physical rotating dial let you choose a station number at hardware level. Some pics here, but not the models I knew: https://www.bcsatellite.net/blog/pats-memoirs-design-time/ Because there was no display, that part of the 80186 memory map could be used for RAM, so a 3Server could give 800-900kB of RAM to DOS. A selling point: it could have 25% more memory than a PC and was arguably easier to configure. The 3Server3 had for the 1980s very high memory limits, but we didn't sell many. 3Com's DOS apps had their own pre-CUA text-mode windowing and menuing system, 3+Menus, with a consistent UI and navigation keys, before Windows 2.0. Fill in fields in any order, Enter to accept, Ctrl+Enter to accept the whole dialog box, close it (with an animated zoom-out effect), and return to the previous level. This applied to all 3Com software and meant very fast navigation. Last seen in the DOS setup tool for the 3C589 ISA NIC. As well as file and print, it bundled an email server client, which almost none of my clients ever used, and it also could act as a network gateway, with tools for WAN linking of networks into a big MAN, which I also never used. I remember putting 3+Share on an IBM PS/2 Model 80 with the biggest hard disk I'd ever seen at that time: 330MB, on an ESDI interface. I had to partition it as drives C:, D:, E:, F:, G:, H:, I:, J:, K: and L:. All 32MB except for an 11MB L: drive. NOS on C:, main network app on the next letter, data on the next letter, home directories on the next, print spools on the next... it tool some ingenuity to find ways to use them all on DOS 3.3. There was only one supported big-partition tool, VFeature Deluxe from Golden Bow Systems, and none of my clients were willing to pay for it. GBS did various DOS addons: a software disk cache, VCache; a defragmenter, VOpt; and VFeature, for disk partitions over 32MB. https://golden-bow-systems.software.informer.com/ I even tried installing it on Compaq DOS 3.31 which had big FAT16 partition support using the same system that MS-DOS 4 later adopted, but 3+Share could not see the big drives.

The difference between TDM and packet switching is the same as between static memory allocation and dynamically allocating heap memory. If you can afford to allocate statically the space for all the variables that your program will ever use, you will certainly increase a lot both the performance and the reliability of your program. Alas, for many tasks this would result in a requirement for more memory than you can afford, especially today. To use more efficiently the limited amount of memory that you have, you need to use dynamic memory allocation. The same happens with your communication infrastructure. Using it with packet switching reduces the reliability and the performance of individual communications, but it uses the capacity much more efficiently, i.e. the aggregated throughput of all communications passing through a given infrastructure is greatly increased.

It's a well-known effect in the study of creativity. And it's not just the presence of significant physical or engineering constraints, even the presence of minor arbitrary constraints can spark creativity in unrelated aspects of the work. For example, 'Weekend Film' competitions have long introduced minor arbitrary constraints only announced at the start to prevent pre-work, such as "Blue socks must be seen and at least one character must have an accent". Often, the socks would be only be seen in the background for a few frames and the accented character would be a passerby overheard for 2 seconds, yet filmmakers, judges and audiences found the presence of the constraints caused all the projects to be more creatively diverse in completely unrelated ways. Interestingly, the effect doesn't have one name. Artists and designers have terms for it, cognitive psychologists have another term, behavioral/organizational sciences and engineering/innovation research each have their own literature as well.

For those not in the know the nearfield is where the balance between the magnetic and electric component of the electromagnetic wave is not yet settled into an equilibrium. It's generally considered about 1/10th of wavelength around the emitter. For 100 MHz the can's walls are certainly near field though at 1.5 GHz nearfield is only ~2cm. Light interactions are generally completely reciprocal and transmitting is the same as receiving. You can measure the properties of a system either by receiving or transmitting from two points and switch them around. There are some non-reciprocal mediums like arrangements of magnetic ferrites caused by zeeman splitting but that doesn't apply here. But what does apply is that if the radio source were coming from a far field source like (~a km+ away, so tens of thousands of wavelengths) then it's electric and magnetic components would be in equilibrium when it hit the somewhat imperfect conducting surface of the can and then coupled through the seam in attenuated form. The stuff inside the can would then be exposed in the near field generated by that balanced far field wave coupling in. This convolution of the balanced far field wave and the coupling through the imperfect seam is different than the convolution of an imbalanced EM wave generated inside in the near field and coupling out through the seam. It's hard to say if it'd be better or worse for the stuff inside though. I think this handwave can ignore the slight non-reciprocity.

I worked in games from 2006 to 2014 on titles that I imagine are similar in scale & production to Oddworld or Dungeon Siege to something more like an EA or Rockstar flagship title towards the end of my career in the industry. On the latter end of my career we had dedicated build/release teams, dedicated mocap technicians, networking/multiplayer teams, international/distributed teams, finer-grained tools teams, dedicated DLC teams, etc. It was a completely different environment. I admittedly don't know firsthand what Thief or Dungeon Siege were like but you can see the difference on Mobygames; these both have ~250-300 credited in total versus Assassin's Creed (and "only" the 2007 version) which has ~900 — it only goes up from there. This is not a rock solid comparison but it's probably a decent proxy to describe the scale of production. You could maybe argue that a title like Assassin's Creed had a bloated team, but as an IC that's not really in my control. But in more concrete terms what I mean is that in the Dungeon Siege/Oddword environment, sure I could have maybe said to my team — I'm going to rewrite "x" because it's not efficient enough, and then go heads down for a while and try to solve this problem. I didn't have that same luxury at the other end of the spectrum. On a smaller team I could maybe say — hey, I think we should drop C++/OOP because of "reasons", and have a somewhat realistic chance of persuading the team. This was unlikely to be taken seriously at your EA/R* type company. Beyond the games industry I'm not going to be taken seriously suggesting to my big tech employer to rewrite everything in Rust instead of Java because OO is evil or it's non-performant or whatever. As far as polymorphism and clean code go, I sometimes find value in leveraging these if they make sense. I may anticipate some persistence-layer migration in the future or feel defensive about the next few intern project and want to try and have some sort of guardrails to limit their blast-radius. Virtual functions are non-performant, Jon or Casey may argue, and they'd be right in their respective domain — but it's not really applicable in mine; even if I were to theoretically drive _my_ service latency down to zero, my end-user would notice no difference as most of the latency is spent on downstream services. Docker is a workaround for the lack of coordination that occurs when there's no ownership of things. Other operating systems have no equivalent of Docker because they don't need it. Consider macOS. The closest equivalent to a container is the bundle. Bundles are much better that containers in several ways: 1. They're much simpler. Just directories with a special structure that's recognized by the OS. 2. They're much more efficient. A bundle ships only the program and any dependencies that sit outside the OS, but Apple invests so much in developing frameworks and in backwards compatibility, that a huge range of apps can be built that require no additional dependencies whatsoever. It's common for sophisticated Mac GUI apps to have bundle sizes in the tens of megabytes, whereas Docker images often require pulling gigabytes. 3. They're decentralized. There is no de-facto reliance on a collection of hubs which charge lots of money for bandwidth (some companies block Docker Hub for this reason). Nor is bundle identity allocated by registries - you can create a bundle with a stable identity that survives upgrades even if you pass the bundles around on SD cards. 4. They're actually more "UNIX philosophy". You can move them around and organize them in the same way as any other kind of file or directory. You can "cd" into them from the shell, or synchronize them with Google Drive. There is no need for special servers, repositories, pulls or pushes. 5. They have much better support for sandboxing. 6. They share the same namespaces as the host, so there are no confusing path remappings going on. Despite that, sandboxed app get private areas of the user's home directory that are protected from other apps. The underlying architecture here isn't perfect; bundles evolved over a period of decades and there's no rigid spec for the internal directory layout. The OS relies on collections of heuristics to identify bundles in a few cases. But it's architecturally much cleaner than Docker.

What you're describing is an "IT systems analyst", or rather, the term "systems analyst" as it evolved into a particular niche usage within IT. But there's a more general kind of "systems analyst" that still survives (and is mostly what the BLS stats refer to): a person whose job is to map out the current business domain of a system (consisting of not just computers, but also people, infrastructure, institutions, etc.) and identify where it will need to be modified (but not necessarily how it will need to be modified) to make it capable of being put to use in a certain way for a given plan/mission. Systems analysts in this sense tend to be one of the actual workhorse jobs inside "management consulting" firms and "think tanks." Governments, militaries, and large bureaucracies with many independent business units (think IBM) are their customers. Systems analysis is sometimes done structurally over an entire organization: someone at a very high level has some new vision for an initiative, and hires these companies/think-tanks to help them determine how to "align" their organizational architecture with what a military might call a new "doctrine" or a company might call a new "paradigm." In these cases, the systems analyst performs the first step of that alignment: understanding "the system as it is today", and identifying what parts of it are already aligned vs. which parts will need to change. Their output is a report to the person driving the process. But structural analysis is more often applied to specific strategic/business units, as the result of that strategic/business unit being chosen to execute a given strategic mission, as an enablement process to get that unit into the specific shape it needs to be in to execute that mission. In this case, there is likely an assigned "mission {planner, architect}" (who may also become the mission's director ; or who may hire for such a director role and then depart to go plan the next mission.) The systems analyst works for/with the mission planner as their "eyes and ears", interacting with the business unit to gather information for the planner to use. In both the structural and strategic cases, there are usually also one or more systems engineers who determine the "how" for implementation of these changes. (A mission planner is usually a very senior systems engineer themselves.) However, unlike the systems analyst, who is considered more trustworthy to central leadership when they exist outside of the system they're analyzing (and so mostly work for external firms like think-tanks rather than for the orgs themselves), there's much less of a motivation to separate out systems engineering in that manner. So systems engineers (including mission planners!) tend to be regular [if high-paid] career employees of the central organization. These folks are frequently "general staff" in a military (with no real analogous term, AFAIK, for the equivalent people within a conglomerate's parent company.) Due to their value coming in part from existing in separate firms that can negotiate on their behalf, systems analysts in this sense are well-paid indeed! But also worked hard, bounced around, and signing NDAs constantly. And possibly a bit bitter, in that they often see how things are broken with no chance to be part of the fix.

"Waterfall" is a pastiche of mature development practices used by Agilists to sell their programmer-centric snake oil. It's basically a phased development process kinda like PRIDE, but it explicitly doesn't incorporate feedback between the phases. PRIDE explicitly allows, for instance, new requirements discovered during the design phase to feed back into the analysis phase. But it is explicitly based on the idea that "A system is a product that can be designed and manufactured, just like any other product." And that the exact same management principles from the manufacturing and construction industries apply to information systems development. It is always a phased process that starts with requirements—identifying what the needs are, followed by design—producing a blueprint of how those needs will be met. This is how bridges, buildings, cars, and consumer goods are built; why not systems? Milt Bryce used to say, "If this country built bridges the way it builds systems, we'd be a nation run by ferryboats." A counter to this is "requirements change quickly, therefore the system needs to change quickly too." But the actual case is: most organizations don't really know how to do systems analysis. So this results in one of two scenarios: either the organization wastes a lot of time and money in the analysis phase struggling to do what they cannot, or they punt on requirements analysis altogether and wait for requirements to surface at implementation time. This is called "Agile" today, but was described by Milt in 1983: "do a superficial feasibility study, do some quick and dirty systems design, spend a lot of time in programming, install prematurely so you can irritate the users sooner, and then keep working on it till you get something accomplished." PRIDE is like a textbook on how to build a system, from requirements analysis through design, implementation, and maintenance. It was the first methodology for doing so, and it transformed information systems from arcane art into a proven, repeatable science. It should be the industry standard, but is now at risk of being forgotten, largely due to programmers holding the industry hostage. AI is taking programmers out of the equation. PRIDE is relevant again.

Thanks for a thoughtful reply. « Hitler's invasion into Poland … Humanitarian » There's no such thing as a "humanitarian military invasion". There were pogroms against Germans in Poland, and thousands of refugees seeking shelter in the Reich, so there were humanitarian issues, and there were reasons to do something about it urgently. But military action never makes anything better. What was going on was somebody provoking Hitler into war. There were of course contingency plans. Hitler wanted to solve the issues involving Poland (Danzig, corridor, and human rights), if possible peacefully (and he made very reasonable proposals: referendum etc) but if not militarily. To then go to war is of course Hitler's hence Germany's responsibility, just like making it into a World War is Britain's. « Lebensraum » — Completely irrelevant for the war, misleading, ex post projection. « Poland had no right to exist as a nation » — Where did you get that from? Hitler wanted an alliance with Poland to protect against Bolshevism. But that was before the anti-German riots. « fundamental text of Nazism » — Completely irrelevant for the war, written in 1924, likely conceived by Hanfstaengl anyway (who was sort of Hitler's mentor). Consider the educational background of Hitler, his biography, his social status. He was a nobody. Not dumb, but a nobody. « fundamental driver was ideological » — It never is. But that's almost always the pretext. "Our values" etc, all that BS. It's always power politics. « just a random Senator » — Not sure there is such a thing. It's not a lottery. You need to be loyal to and affiliated with the power basis. And that is not the people, but the rich families who own the country. « that the invasion was a spontaneous reaction to something that was happening in Poland then? » There's no such thing as a spontaneous invasion. It has to be prepared, and it had been prepared as "plan B", because Hitler wanted to solve the issues fast , and by force if need be. But he tried to solve them by perfectly peaceful and democratic means (referendum etc) so there could be peaceful coexistence and Poland would obtain a port on the Baltic, whatever the outcome. A peaceful settlement was not in Britain's interest, so they torpedoed that solution, bolstering up Poland. And incredible as it sounds today, leading Polish politicians such as Beck thought that if push came to shove there would a putsch or revolution against Hitler in Germany and the Polish army would march in unter den Linden . Passkeys as they are currently-marketed are resident credentials. This means a passkey stored on your Yubikey (or smartphone, or Windows account, or...) is not only a private key, but also contains a UID to identify it. A website doing authentication can trivially use this to look up which user it is associated with. Very convenient for single-press login, but it requires a decent bunch of per-website storage on the hardware token. Which is of course a net positive for the big tech companies, because it forced you into using smartphones as the token, and doing silly things like cloud sync with them. The original FIDO U2F credentials were not resident. You'd enter your username, and the website would sent over a bunch of opaque blobs representing the associated hardware tokens. The hardware token would decrypt their blob using a key derived from a combination of the website's domain name and the hardware token's single stored secret, and then do the whole auth shenanigans using the data retrieved from the blob.

Consider that you can't move files around in /proc, although you can with any real file. You can't hard link them or put your own files next to them or add xattrs or change their ownership. Procfs is basically just a crappy untyped API that requires tons of ad hoc non automated parsing code to use. Other operating systems haven't copied it because it's not a particularly good feature.

Hello HN, I am Ioannis and I would like to introduce Logonomic, a desktop application we made to help us work with LLM CLIs (e.g. codex, claude, opencode etc) in a more organized way. It runs the CLIs already installed, with their existing accounts and configuration and organizes sessions by repository. It is available for Windows and Linux, with a preview for macOS. There is also a mobile companion app, to work remotely (Android and soon iOS too). We built it originally to assist us in our own work, to address the common case of multiple agents running concurrently in many repositories. It was hard to keep track of what each one is doing and which one needs attention or requires action. There are many tools by now broadly that broadly target the same problem. This one is a native C++/Qt application with our own terminal emulator. Some of its features: - An 'overview' mode that shows all running sessions, optionally grouped by repository, each with its status, title and summary that the agents update regularly. - Agents add a trailer to their commits, enabling to re-open the conversations that produced them. - Terminals run in their own processes and survive UI crashes. - A plot that shows line counts over time, by directory or language, where clicking on a sample brings up the corresponding commit in the git log. - A treemap that shows how the repo's files are organized, with a diff mode that colours changed files, whose diff opens with a double click. - Token usage and remaining account quotas shown where available, with usage broken down by day and repository. - Sessions can exchange messages (1:1 or broadcast), may hand tasks to each other or continue other session's work. The supported CLIs are Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode, Antigravity, Grok Build, Kimi Code and Qwen Code. The free edition has no time limit and runs up to four terminals. The paid editions have perpetual one-time licences from €150 for 2 seats and include 12 months of feature updates, no terminal limit, GitHub/GitLab CI integrations, as well as an Android companion app (iOS will follow). The application itself is proprietary. Many of its core components are open source, among them the terminal emulator and the plotting library: https://github.com/Varinomics This is the first public release, so there will be rough edges, and we would like to hear about them.
